nameStory: The single-dotted wave gets its name from the distinctive single dot or spot that appears on each of its forewings, combined with the wavy lines that ripple across its wings like gentle waves on water. Many moths in the wave family have multiple dots or no dots at all, making this species' solitary marking its calling card.
description: The single-dotted wave is a small, delicate moth in the geometer family, known for their caterpillars that move by arching their bodies in a looping motion. This dainty moth has pale, cream-colored to light brown wings decorated with subtle wavy lines and that telltale single dark spot on each forewing. Adults typically have a wingspan of about three-quarters of an inch to one inch across, making them quite petite compared to many other moths you might encounter at your porch light.

idTips.label: Single dark spot
idTips.description: Look for one distinct dark dot on each forewing - this is the most reliable identifying feature and won't be found on other similar wave moths

idTips.label: Wavy wing lines
idTips.description: Delicate, undulating lines cross the wings horizontally, giving them a subtle rippled appearance like sand patterns on a beach

idTips.label: Wing color
idTips.description: Wings range from pale cream to light grayish-brown, often with a slightly translucent quality that shows through when backlit

idTips.label: Body size
idTips.description: Small and slender with a wingspan typically less than an inch - you could easily cover one with a quarter

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings have a soft, powdery feel typical of moths, with fine scales that can rub off on your fingers if handled

habitat: Single-dotted waves can be found in a variety of open and semi-open habitats across New England, including gardens, meadows, woodland edges, and areas with mixed vegetation. They're particularly common around human settlements where outdoor lights attract them at night. Look for them in areas with diverse plant communities, as their caterpillars feed on various low-growing plants and organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, becoming active as temperatures warm and days lengthen.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when adults are most commonly seen attracted to lights at night and can be found resting on vegetation during the day.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with some individuals still flying on warm evenings before the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active during winter months, likely overwintering as eggs or pupae in protected locations.

funFact: Despite being called a 'wave' moth, the single-dotted wave is actually found across the entire northern hemisphere - from New England all the way to Europe and Asia - making it one of the most widely distributed small moths in the world!
confusionNotes: The single-dotted wave can be confused with other small, pale wave moths, but the single dark spot on each forewing is your foolproof identifier - remember 'one dot, one species.' Other wave moths either have multiple spots, no spots at all, or different patterns entirely.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'geometer' comes from Greek meaning 'earth measurer,' referring to how the caterpillars appear to be measuring the ground as they loop along - they're also called inchworms or loopers for this distinctive walking style.
compareHints: Since this is the only Idaea species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small wave moths in the geometer family. Most other waves lack the single distinctive dot, instead showing either no spots, multiple spots, or completely different wing patterns. The single-dotted wave's combination of pale coloring, wavy lines, and that lone dark spot makes it unique among New England's small moths.
